title: Atoms and isotopes

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Proton
items.clue: A positively charged particle found in the nucleus.

items.label: Plum pudding model
items.clue: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

items.label: Indivisible sphere model
items.clue: The early idea that atoms were tiny balls that could not be split.

items.label: Bohr model
items.clue: Electrons orbit at specific distances from the centre of the atom.

questions.stem: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?

options.text: Its neutrons cancel out the charge of the protons
It has just as many electrons as it has neutrons
Its charges are much too small to be noticed
It has equal numbers of protons and electrons

questions.explanation: In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons, so the charges cancel.

questions.stem: What is the atomic number of an element?

options.text: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of protons and neutrons added
The number of electrons in the outer shell
The number of neutrons in the nucleus

questions.explanation: The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number.

questions.stem: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?

options.text: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of the atom
The number of protons and electrons in the atom
The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
The mass of a single atom, measured in grams

questions.explanation: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom is called its mass number.

questions.stem: An atom of sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?

options.text: 11 neutrons, since 11 is the smaller number
34 neutrons, found from 23 + 11 = 34
23 neutrons, the larger of the numbers
12 neutrons, worked out from 23 - 11 = 12

questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.

questions.stem: In the conventional representation of an atom, what does the lower number stand for?

options.text: The atomic number, which counts the protons
The mass number, the protons plus the neutrons
The number of neutrons found inside the nucleus
The charge held by the nucleus in coulombs

questions.explanation: The lower number is the atomic number: the number of protons in the atom.

questions.stem: What are isotopes of an element?

options.text: Atoms which have different numbers of protons
Atoms with equal protons, unequal neutrons
Atoms of the element that have lost an electron
Atoms of two different elements with the same mass

questions.explanation: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.

questions.stem: How does an atom turn into a positive ion?

options.text: By gaining one or more electrons from elsewhere
By gaining one extra proton into its nucleus
By losing one neutron from its own nucleus
By losing one or more electrons from its outer shell

questions.explanation: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electrons.

questions.stem: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. Which statement about them is correct?

options.text: They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers
They have different atomic numbers and different mass numbers
They have the same mass number but a different charge
They have different numbers of electrons in an atom

questions.explanation: Isotopes of an element share the proton number and therefore the atomic number, but differ in neutrons and so in mass number.

questions.stem: A lithium atom with mass number 7 and atomic number 3 loses one electron. What is the resulting ion?

options.text: Charge -1, because one electron has been removed
Charge +1, mass number is still 7, 3 protons
Charge +1, mass number 6, with 3 protons still
Charge +1, mass number 8, a proton joined

questions.explanation: Losing one electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the charge is +1. The nucleus is untouched, so mass number 7 and 3 protons remain.
